title: Development of chromium nitride layers on Inconel 625: impact on structural integrity and chemical stability
abstract: Abstract This study evaluated the surface modification of Inconel 625 superalloy by conventional plasma nitriding (PN) and cathode cage plasma nitriding (CCPN), performed at 450 °C and 500 °C for 5 h. The samples were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), microhardness testing under 50 gf for 15 s, roughness measurements, adhesion testing under 150 kgf, potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, and pin-on-disc wear testing against an AISI 52,100 steel ball under 5 N for 3000 s. The results confirmed the formation of the CrN phase under all treatment conditions. Surface hardness increased after nitriding, with the CC500 condition reaching 1573.57 HV, corresponding to a 383.7% increase compared with the untreated alloy. Adhesion tests indicated satisfactory performance, especially for the CC450 condition, which was classified as HF1. From an electrochemical standpoint, the treatments shifted the surface behavior toward more noble potentials, with PN450 showing the lowest corrosion current density of 3.71 × 10 − 9  mA cm − 2 . Tribological performance was also improved, as the nitrided samples showed reduced disk wear and promoted the formation of protective Fe- and O-rich tribofilms during sliding. Therefore, PN and CCPN show high potential for naval components, representing efficient and sustainable alternatives to improve the durability of Inconel 625 in marine environments.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The exploitation of natural resources in marine environments requires structures and components with chemical and structural stability under harsh conditions, exposing their materials to mechanical and tribological stresses and corrosive environments [ 1 ,  2 ]. A commonly adopted alternative to minimize the effects of the marine environment is the production of hard electrolytic chromium coatings (EHC) [ 3 ,  4 ]. However, these coatings often exhibit numerous microscopic cracks due to stresses generated during formation [ 5 ].

Hard chromium coatings are traditionally obtained by electrolytic processes, which release fumes containing hexavalent chromium (Cr 6+ ), recognized for its carcinogenic potential [ 6 ]. Due to these health risks, regulatory agencies have intensified restrictions on the use of this technology [ 7 ]. Other techniques have therefore been employed to promote the deposition of hard coatings that are resistant to wear and corrosion in marine environments, without emitting gases harmful to human health [ 6 ]. ID-HVOF spraying is an alternative to electrodeposited hard chromium (EHC) processing and has been used for complex geometries applied in aeronautics, such as landing gear and fuselage components [ 8 ], as well as in the naval industry [ 9 ], the automotive sector [ 10 ], and several other applications. However, this technique requires high-cost and complex equipment.

Two more economical alternatives that offer greater process control for tailoring the surface properties of naval mechanical components are conventional plasma nitriding (PN) and cathodic cage plasma nitriding (CCPN). Widely reported in the literature, PN and CCPN are thermochemical processes carried out at low pressure in a nitrogen-containing atmosphere that can promote surface modifications on metals, metallic alloys, and steels. These modifications can lead to significant performance improvements, including increased surface hardness and enhanced wear and corrosion resistance, even when forming layers or coatings thinner than those typically obtained by ID-HVOF spraying [ 11 ,  12 ,  13 – 14 ].

Skobir Balantič et al. (2023) performed plasma nitriding on Inconel 625 produced by additive manufacturing (LPBF) and by conventional processing, using a 75% H 2 –25% N 2  atmosphere at 430 °C and 500 °C for 15 h. The temperature of 430 °C promoted the formation of expanded austenite, whereas at 500 °C, intense precipitation of chromium nitrides (CrN) occurred, increasing surface hardness but reducing corrosion resistance due to local chromium depletion. In contrast, wear resistance was significantly improved at both nitriding temperatures [ 15 ]. On the other hand, A. F. S. do M. e Silva et al. (2026) performed conventional plasma nitriding (PN) and cathodic cage plasma nitriding (CCPN) on AISI 420 martensitic stainless steel at 400, 450, and 500 °C for 5 h. The results highlighted that CCPN achieves an optimized balance between hardness and interfacial integrity, with excellent adhesion and corrosion protection superior to those of the untreated substrate. In addition, the CCPN process favors the progressive stabilization of the surface in saline media by depositing sputtered particles from the cage, resulting in stable protective layers without compromising the material’s internal microstructure [ 16 ].

In this context, this work investigates the surface modification of Inconel 625 superalloy by conventional plasma nitriding (PN) and cathodic cage plasma nitriding (CCPN), performed at 450 and 500 °C, aiming to improve its performance under marine-environment conditions. The originality of this study lies in the direct comparison between PN and CCPN applied to Inconel 625, using a cathodic cEke age made of the same alloy as a source of sputtered species to promote the formation of CrN-rich surface layers without conventional hard chromium electroplating. Unlike previous studies that focused mainly on additively manufactured Inconel 625 or stainless-steel substrates, this work provides an integrated assessment of layer formation, phase evolution, surface hardness, adhesion, and corrosion behavior in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, and sliding wear performance. This approach allows the relationships among surface hardening, layer integrity, electrochemical stability, and tribofilm formation to be highlighted, highlighting the potential of these treatments to enhance the durability and reliability of Inconel 625 naval components.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: Inconel 625 samples, a nickel–chromium superalloy with the following composition (wt%): 59.5% Ni, 22% Cr, 9% Mo, 5% Fe, and 4.5% Ta, Mn, and Si, were fabricated with dimensions of 20 × 20 × 1 mm. These samples underwent surface standardization using sandpapers with grit sizes ranging from 220 to 1200 mesh and were subsequently polished with a polishing cloth using 0.3 μm alumina as the abrasive. Finally, the samples were subjected to ultrasonic agitation in 99% ethanol and dried with a hot-air jet.

The samples were subjected to two types of plasma treatment: conventional plasma nitriding (PN) and cathodic cage plasma nitriding (CCPN) using an Inconel 625 cage. A schematic representation of the sample positioning during the PN and CCPN treatments is shown in Fig.  1 .
Fig. 1 Schematic representation of the sample positioning during the treatments: ( a ) conventional plasma nitriding and ( b ) cathodic cage plasma nitriding

The treatments were carried out in a plasma reactor comprising a chamber connected to a DC power supply rated at 1200 V and 2 A, and a vacuum system equipped with a mechanical pump, pressure sensors, and flow controllers. A thermocouple inserted inside the sample holder rod, as shown in Fig.  1 , was used to measure the sample temperature during the plasma treatments. The system used in this work has been extensively described in previous studies [ 16 ]. Before the treatments, a pre-sputtering step was performed for 1 h in an atmosphere of 50 sccm argon and 50 sccm hydrogen at 350 °C and a pressure of approximately 3.2 × 10 2  Pa to promote surface cleaning prior to modification by PN and CCPN. After this step, the treatment parameters were adjusted to initiate nitriding. The sample nomenclature and processing parameters are presented in Table  1 .

Table 1 Parameters used in the pre-sputtering step and in the PN and CCPN processes Samples Plasma treatments type of processing temperature (°C) pressure (Pa) time (h) gas flow (sccm) UNT - - - - - PN450 PN 450 1.2 × 10 3 5 25N 2 /75H 2 PN500 500 1.1 × 10 3 CC450 CCPN 450 3.0 × 10 2 60N 2 /40H 2 CC500 500 3.0 × 10 2

The crystalline structure of the Inconel 625 samples was analyzed using a Bruker D2 PHASER X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.1541 nm), a step size of 0.01°, and a 2θ range of 20°- 80°. The diffractograms were refined using the Rietveld method in TOPAS 4.2. The cross-sectional microstructure of the samples subjected to plasma treatments was evaluated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) using a FEI COMPANY QUANTA FEG 250 microscope operated at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV. The thickness of the nitrided layers was measured in five distinct regions using ImageJ software. Surface hardness was determined by Vickers microhardness testing (HV) using an INSIZE ISH-TDV 1000 A-B microhardness tester, with a load of 50 gf and a dwell time of 15 s. Five measurements were performed to obtain the mean and standard deviation, in accordance with ASTM E384 [ 17 ]. Surface roughness was evaluated using a portable Mitutoyo Surftest SJ-210 roughness tester. For each sample, five measurements were taken at different surface locations, and the arithmetic mean roughness (Ra) and root-mean-square roughness (Rq) were determined according to ISO 21920-2 [ 18 ]. The adhesion of the nitrided layer to the nickel–chromium superalloy substrate was evaluated using an Insize Rockwell-C hardness tester (model ISH-BRV) with a 150 kgf load, in accordance with ISO 6508-1. The Daimler-Benz scale (HF0–HF6) was adopted in accordance with BS ISO 26443:2016 [ 19 ].

Corrosion tests were performed using a three-electrode system in a glass cell containing a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. A saturated Ag/AgCl/KCl reference electrode was used to obtain the potentiodynamic polarization curves. The measurements were started at − 400 mV and stopped when the current density reached 1 mA cm − 2 , with a scan rate of 1 mV s − 1 . The open circuit potential (OCP) was measured for 60 s before each potentiodynamic polarization measurement to stabilize the system. Wear analysis was carried out using a pin-on-disk test with an AISI 52,100 steel ball, 6 mm in diameter, attached to the pin. The tests were performed under a constant normal load of 5 N, a sliding speed of 5 cm s⁻¹, a wear radius of 8 mm, and a rotation rate of 60 rpm for 3000 s. The wear morphology was characterized by scanning electron microscopy.

sections.heading: X-ray diffraction analysis and Rietveld method
paragraphs: The X-ray diffraction analysis of the nickel-based superalloy sample, Inconel 625, is presented in Fig.  2 . The diffractogram of the untreated sample shows three characteristic NiCr peaks at 2θ positions of 43.39° (111), 50.56° (002), and 74.22° (022) [ 20 ], in agreement with the ICSD 102,819 standard [ 21 ]. The Rietveld method was applied to the experimental data to obtain a high-quality numerical fit, as evidenced by the GOF (Goodness of Fit) value of 1.06 and the low-amplitude residual curve (Difference).
Fig. 2 X-ray diffractogram of the untreated Inconel 625 sample

The Inconel 625 samples subjected to plasma nitriding processes, PN and CCPN, also exhibited the NiCr peaks highlighted in Fig.  2 . However, the presence of the CrN phase, ICSD standard 192,945, was also observed as a result of the plasma nitriding processes. It is noteworthy that, despite the higher nickel content in the Inconel 625 superalloy, chromium nitride is preferentially formed during plasma nitriding. This behavior is associated with chromium’s chemical affinity for nitrogen and the lower free-energy formation of this nitride compared with those of possible nickel and molybdenum nitrides. The CrN bond energy is 400 kJ/mol, and its more negative Gibbs free energy (ΔG° ≈ −90 kJ/mol) justifies the formation of this nitride rather than Ni and Mo nitrides [ 22 ]. According to M. Kim and S. Lee (2025), nitrogen adsorbed on the Ni surface is energetically less stable than gaseous N 2 . Therefore, the formation of nickel nitrides becomes unfavorable, despite the alloy containing 59.5% Ni [ 23 ]. Nickel exhibits low stability in forming nitride compounds and therefore remains in the matrix phase. Although molybdenum can form nitrides, its lower fraction and thermodynamic disadvantage relative to chromium also limit its formation and detection.

Figure  3  presents the diffractograms and their respective Rietveld fits. GOF values close to 1.00 confirm the quality of the refinement procedure and enable quantitative evaluation of the analyzed microstructures.
Fig. 3 X-ray diffractograms of the samples subjected to PN and CCPN processes with Rietveld refinement fitting: ( a ) PN450, ( b ) PN500, ( c ) CC450, and ( d ) CC500

The quantitative results obtained by Rietveld refinement, presented in Table  2 , show the structural parameter a (Å) and unit cell volume (Å 3 ) for the cubic NiCr and CrN phases in the samples analyzed by X-ray diffraction. Table  2  evidences a reduction in the lattice parameter  a  and, consequently, in the unit cell volume of the NiCr phase, indicating lattice contraction of the matrix. This behavior may be attributed to compositional redistribution resulting from the preferential consumption of chromium during the formation of the CrN phase during plasma nitriding at 450 and 500 °C, leading to local depletion of this element in the NiCr matrix. Additionally, nitride formation and process-related effects, such as ion bombardment and thermal gradients, contribute to the introduction of compressive residual stresses, which may also influence the reduction in lattice parameters [ 24 ]. The reduction in the lattice parameter tends to increase lattice distortion, hindering dislocation motion and, consequently, increasing surface hardness [ 25 ]. On the other hand, the presence of the CrN phase, with a cubic structure and lattice parameters close to those reported in the literature, indicates the formation of a stable surface nitride layer associated with superior mechanical properties [ 26 ].

Table 2 Lattice parameters, crystallite size, and phase fraction results obtained by the Rietveld refinement method Samples Phase Structural parameters Refinement results a(Å) Cell vol. (Å 3 ) Cry. Size (D) (nm) Phase (%) GOF UNT NiCr 3.611 47.10 228.1 100 1.06 PN450 NiCr 3.556 44.99 6.3 39.33 1.14 CrN 4.149 71.42 6.4 60.67 PN500 NiCr 3.539 44.34 4.2 53.24 1.02 CrN 4.178 72.95 3.9 46.76 CC450 NiCr 3.542 44.44 11.3 39.86 1.13 CrN 4.161 72.08 7.4 60.14 CC500 NiCr 3.541 44.43 13.3 39.93 1.19 CrN 4.158 71.89 9.0 71.89

Table  2  also presents the crystallite size (D) results for all phases present in the analyzed samples. The crystallite size of 228.1 nm for the NiCr phase in the untreated sample indicates a low density of crystalline defects. However, the samples nitrided by the PN technique exhibited phases with smaller crystallite sizes. The PN450 and PN500 samples showed D values of 6.3 nm and 4.2 nm, respectively. The reduction in D may be attributed to an increase in defects generated during plasma nitriding, which was intensified by raising the temperature from 450 to 500 °C. Since the samples are at cathodic potential, direct ion bombardment of the surface occurs, favoring the introduction of crystalline defects and residual stresses [ 27 ]. The samples subjected to the CCPN process exhibited phases with larger crystallite sizes than those observed in the PN-treated samples. For the CC450 sample, the NiCr and CrN phases showed D = 11.3 nm and D = 7.4 nm, respectively, whereas for the CC500 sample, these values were D = 13.3 nm for the NiCr phase and D = 9.0 nm for the CrN phase. Although these results still indicate significant microstructural refinement relative to the untreated alloy, as evidenced by a reduction in crystallite size and a consequent increase in crystalline defect density, the higher values compared with the PN-treated samples suggest that the CCPN process promotes a less defective structure. This behavior may be attributed to the presence of the cathodic cage, which tends to attenuate the effects of direct ion bombardment, while also favoring a more homogeneous energy distribution and greater thermal stability on the sample surface.

The phase fractions of each sample are also presented in Table  2 . The variation in CrN content may be associated with the kinetics of nitrided layer formation during conventional plasma nitriding (PN), which are influenced by higher process temperatures. At higher temperatures, intensified ion bombardment of the surface favors not only nitrogen incorporation but also sputtering of the surface material [ 28 ]. This removal process competes with the formation of the nitrided phase, potentially reducing the effective thickness of the formed layer. As a consequence, lower detection of the CrN phase by XRD is observed, due to the greater relative contribution of the NiCr substrate phase within the analyzed volume. The CrN contents of the samples subjected to CCPN indicate surface-modification kinetics with a less pronounced sputtering effect. This may justify the formation of a thicker nitride layer and, consequently, a higher amount of CrN detected by the Rietveld method.

sections.heading: Cross-sectional micrograph and surface roughness
paragraphs: Figure  4  presents cross-sectional micrographs of the plasma-nitrided samples, evidencing the formation of surface nitrided layers attributed to the CrN phase on the Inconel 625 alloy. The average thickness values indicate that the samples subjected to conventional plasma nitriding (PN) exhibited thinner layers, with values of 5.33 ± 0.92 μm for PN450 and 2.91 ± 0.31 μm for PN500. This behavior is consistent with the phase-fraction results from Rietveld refinement, which showed a reduction in the detected CrN fraction with increasing temperature during the PN process. This effect may be associated with intensified ion bombardment of the surface, as the samples were held at cathodic potential, which favors surface sputtering. Thus, the material removal process competes with the formation of the nitrided layer, reducing its thickness and, consequently, the contribution of the CrN phase to the volume analyzed by XRD.
Fig. 4 Scanning electron micrographs of the plasma-nitrided samples: ( a ) PN450, ( b ) PN500, ( c ) CC450, and ( d ) CC500

The coatings produced by cathodic cage plasma nitriding (CCPN) exhibited greater thicknesses, with average values of 6.92 ± 0.99 μm for sample CC450 and 7.10 ± 0.54 μm for CC500. These results are consistent with the higher CrN phase fractions observed under these conditions, especially for CC500, indicating greater retention and stability of the formed layer. In addition, the higher crystallite size values obtained for the NiCr and CrN phases in the CC samples, compared with the PN samples, suggest that the cathodic cage process promotes a less aggressive surface modification, with lower defect density and a better balance between nitride formation and structural preservation. Sample CC500, in particular, exhibited a thicker and more uniform layer, indicating greater microstructural homogeneity. This characteristic, associated with the presence of the hard CrN phase and the previously mentioned residual contraction stress in the NiCr matrix resulting from Cr depletion during nitride formation, suggests potential improvements in the surface’s mechanical and tribological behavior, especially under more severe loading conditions.

Other important parameters for describing the surface effects of nitriding processes applied to Inconel 625 are the arithmetic mean roughness (Ra) and the root-mean-square roughness (Rq). While Ra represents the average irregularity of the surface profile, Rq is more sensitive to pronounced peaks and valleys, indicating the severity of these irregularities [ 29 ]. As shown in Fig.  5 , the Ra and Rq parameters exhibit similar trends across the analyzed conditions, indicating that the nitriding treatments consistently modified the samples’ surface topography. The untreated sample (UNT), representative of the initial condition after surface preparation, exhibited the lowest roughness values and the smallest data dispersion, consistent with a smoother, more uniform surface. In contrast, the nitrided samples showed increases in both Ra and Rq, indicating that the treatments promoted topographical changes associated with the growth of the nitrided layer and the effects of ion bombardment during the process. The analysis of the standard deviations further indicates that roughness variation across different surface regions depends on the treatment condition, allowing inference of differences in the degree of homogeneity of the surface modification promoted by the PN and CCPN processes.
Fig. 5 Arithmetic mean roughness (Ra) and root mean square roughness (Rq) of the analyzed samples

In general, the standard deviation decreases as the treatment temperature increases, suggesting that higher temperatures favor a more uniform topographical modification across the surface. Sample PN500 stands out because it exhibited a markedly reduced standard deviation, indicating greater surface homogeneity across the analyzed regions. In addition, the average Ra values for samples nitrided at 450 °C were lower than those for samples treated at 500 °C, suggesting that surface roughness increases with temperature. This behavior should be interpreted in conjunction with the specific characteristics of each process, since the final topography is determined not solely by the treatment temperature but also by the layer-formation kinetics, ion bombardment, and surface-growth mechanisms characteristic of each nitriding condition.

Although the growth of the CrN layer enhances mechanical protection and may improve corrosion resistance, the increased surface roughness associated with the treatment may partially offset this benefit. On rougher surfaces, the increase in the real area exposed to the medium, together with the presence of peaks and valleys, favors the local retention of aggressive species and the formation of microenvironments conducive to the initiation of localized corrosion processes [ 30 ]. Thus, the protective effect of the CrN layer against electrochemical corrosion must be evaluated in balance with the topographical changes induced by the treatment, since increased roughness may limit the system’s corrosion performance.

sections.heading: Surface microhardness and adhesion testing
paragraphs: The Vickers microhardness results, presented in Fig.  6 , showed a significant increase in surface hardness for all nitrided samples, indicating greater resistance to plastic deformation compared with the untreated alloy. Although the coating thicknesses still allow some substrate influence on the hardness values obtained by Vickers indentation, the formation of CrN-rich surface layers led to significant surface hardening. This behavior may be associated with the presence of the hard ceramic phase.

The PN450 and PN500 samples showed increases in hardness of 165.4% and 236.5%, respectively, compared with the untreated sample. Although the PN500 sample exhibited a thinner layer, its higher surface hardness suggests that hardening depends not only on coating thickness but also on the microstructural changes induced by the treatment and on its homogeneity. In this case, this behavior may be associated with greater intensification of crystalline defects, lattice contraction of the NiCr phase, and a smaller crystallite size, as observed in the Rietveld-refined structural results presented in Table  2 . These factors hinder dislocation motion and increase resistance to plastic deformation.

The samples treated by CCPN, in turn, exhibited an average hardness 32.3% higher than that of the samples subjected to the PN process, evidencing the greater efficiency of this treatment in surface hardening of the alloy. Although the CC450 sample showed hardness values close to those of PN500, considering the standard deviations, the CC500 sample stood out, with a 383.7% increase compared with the untreated sample. This result may be attributed to the combination of greater layer thickness and improved homogeneity of the nitrided layer, higher detected CrN fraction, and structural hardening of the surface, which together favored the more pronounced increase in surface hardness.
Fig. 6 Vickers microhardness results of the untreated sample and the samples subjected to conventional plasma nitriding and cathodic cage plasma nitriding

The Rockwell C indentation test was used to evaluate the adhesion of the nitrided layers to the Inconel 625 alloy, according to the Daimler-Benz scale classification (HF0–HF6) [ 31 ,  32 ]. In general, all samples exhibited good adhesion to the substrate, since no evident detachment or delamination was observed around the indentations. However, Fig.  7  shows the formation of radial cracks in all conditions, indicating that, although the coating/substrate interface remained intact, the mechanical response of the layers under localized loading was influenced by the relative brittleness of the formed CrN layer and by the ability of the system to accommodate the stresses generated during indentation. This behavior is consistent with the nitrided coatings exhibiting a significant increase in surface hardness and varying in thickness under the PN and CCPN conditions.

The PN450 sample was classified as HF2, indicating good adhesion, with small cracks and no severe failures around the indentation. The CC450 sample exhibited the best performance, classified as HF1, indicating excellent adhesion and only discrete, almost imperceptible cracks. For samples treated at 500 °C, an increase in radial crack length was observed, particularly in the PN500 sample, which was classified as HF3. This result suggests that, under this condition, the combination of high surface hardness and a lower layer thickness favored greater stress concentration during indentation, thereby increasing susceptibility to crack nucleation and propagation. In other words, the lower coating thickness made the substrate’s mechanical influence more pronounced during the test, increasing the deformation mismatch between the nitrided layer, which exhibits more brittle behavior, and the underlying superalloy, which has greater plastic deformation capacity. On the other hand, the CC500 sample, despite exhibiting the highest surface hardness, was classified as HF2. This behavior may be attributed to the greater thickness and improved homogeneity of the layer formed by CCPN, which favored more efficient stress distribution induced by indentation and reduced the severity of the observed cracking.

The formation of cracks in nitrided coatings is a relevant aspect, even when immediate delamination does not occur. In components subjected to mechanical loading, especially under cyclic loading or localized contact, these cracks can act as stress concentrators and preferential sites for initiating surface damage, thereby favoring the propagation of failure during continued service. Under sliding wear conditions, the presence of cracks may accelerate local fragmentation of the layer, increase debris generation, and favor wear mechanisms associated with brittle fracture and progressive coating detachment. In corrosive environments, these discontinuities may serve as preferential pathways for electrolyte penetration into the layer’s inner regions or toward the interface with the substrate, thereby favoring localized corrosion and partially compromising the protective effect of CrN. Thus, the adhesion results indicate that the best coating performance depends not only on increased hardness but also on a balance among surface hardening, layer thickness, microstructural homogeneity, and resistance to cracking under mechanical loading.
Fig. 7 Adhesion test of the chromium nitride layers formed by PN and CCPN: ( a ) PN450, ( b ) PN500, ( c ) CC450, and ( d ) CC500

sections.heading: Open-circuit potential (OCP) and potentiodynamic polarization curves
paragraphs: The electrochemical test results, especially the open-circuit potential (OCP) shown in Fig.  8 a, allow evaluation of the nitrided layer’s chemical stability in a corrosive environment. It can be observed that all samples subjected to plasma nitriding, both by conventional plasma nitriding (PN) and cathodic cage plasma nitriding (CCPN), reached equilibrium states at significantly more noble potentials than the untreated sample (UNT). This shift toward more positive values indicates that the treatments promoted a surface modification that made the Inconel 625 alloy electrochemically more stable in the corrosive medium [ 33 ]. In principle, this behavior suggests a reduced tendency toward initial corrosion, possibly due to the formation of a CrN-rich surface layer and more favorable conditions for the development of passive films.

The corrosion potential (E corr ) values shown in Fig.  8 b confirm the anodic shift induced by the treatments, particularly for the conventionally nitrided samples PN450 (− 0.039 V) and PN500 (− 0.014 V), relative to the untreated sample UNT (− 0.224 V). This behavior is associated with chemical and structural modifications of the surface after nitriding, particularly the presence of the CrN phase identified by XRD, which can act as a protective barrier and contribute to increasing the surface’s noble character [ 31 ].
Fig. 8 ( a ) Open circuit potential (OCP) and ( b ) potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) curves of the untreated sample and the samples nitrided by PN and CCPN

The analysis of the corrosion current density (J corr ), whose values are presented in Table  3 , provides a more direct evaluation of the material degradation kinetics. The samples treated by PN exhibited the lowest current density values, with 3.71 × 10 − 9  mA/cm 2  for PN450 and 9.45 × 10 − 9  mA/cm 2  for PN500, indicating a significant reduction in the corrosion rate compared with the untreated sample (3.39 × 10 − 8  mA/cm 2 ) [ 34 ,  35 ]. These results show that conventional plasma nitriding was more effective at improving the corrosion resistance of Inconel 625, particularly in the PN450 condition, which exhibited the most positive and stable OCP and the lowest corrosion current density among all analyzed conditions.

Table 3 Electrochemical parameters obtained from the potentiodynamic polarization curves of the analyzed samples Samples E corr  (V) J (mA.cm − 2 ) UNT -0.224 3.39 × 10 − 8 PN450 -0.039 3.71 × 10 − 9 PN500 -0.014 9.4 5 × 10 − 9 CC450 -0.055 3.60 × 10 − 8 CC500 -0.048 2.04 × 10 − 8

In contrast, although the CCPN treatments produced thicker and more microstructurally homogeneous layers, the corrosion current densities obtained for CC450 (3.60 × 10⁻⁸ mA/cm²) and CC500 (2.04 × 10⁻⁸ mA/cm²) remained higher than those observed for the PN samples, approaching, in the case of CC450, the behavior of the untreated alloy. This result indicates that an isolated increase in the thickness of the nitrided layer does not guarantee higher corrosion resistance. The interpretation of these data must also consider the surface topography, as the samples treated by CCPN exhibited higher average roughness, which may have limited the layer’s protective efficiency. Rougher surfaces tend to expose a larger real area to the electrolyte and also favor the local retention of aggressive species in peaks, valleys, and discontinuities [ 30 ]. Under these conditions, roughness intensifies surface electrochemical heterogeneity and favors the onset of localized corrosion. Thus, although the growth of the CrN layer is beneficial for surface hardening and may contribute to electrochemical protection, the simultaneous increase in roughness may partially compromise this benefit, especially when accompanied by topographical defects, cracks, or regions with reduced layer continuity.

The formation of CrN may promote compositional redistribution at the surface, with preferential consumption of chromium from the NiCr matrix, resulting in local depletion of this element in adjacent regions. This Cr depletion may reduce the efficiency of local passivation and make certain regions more susceptible to anodic dissolution, especially at the interfaces between the nitrided layer and the modified matrix. As a consequence, local galvanic microcells may form between more noble regions associated with CrN and chromium-depleted regions, thereby favoring localized corrosion processes [ 30 ]. This interpretation is consistent with the behavior observed in the polarization curves, where some conditions showed a more pronounced increase in current in the anodic region. This current increase indicates lower surface stability under polarization. It suggests greater susceptibility to local breakdown of the passive film (Cr₂O₃) or protective layer, especially at sites associated with topographical heterogeneities, discontinuities, and cracks. Thus, although the electrochemical results alone do not confirm pitting corrosion, they indicate a greater tendency toward localized corrosion under conditions of higher surface roughness and/or more compromised surface chemical integrity.

sections.heading: Tribological test (ball-on-disk) and mass loss
paragraphs: Figure  9  presents scanning electron microscopy images of the worn regions after the ball-on-disk tribological test, together with elemental maps from the wear track on the disk and the wear scar on the ball. The untreated sample (UNT) exhibited a wider wear track, with contrast regions associated with tribofilm formation, likely composed of metallic oxides generated during sliding. The elemental mapping of the wear track indicates a slight reduction in the Ni signal, suggesting partial removal of the Inconel 625 matrix, and the presence of O in regions corresponding to the tribofilm, indicating the participation of tribo-oxidative processes. In contrast, the ball used in contact with the UNT sample exhibited lower wear, with an average scar diameter of 825.23 ± 99.40 μm, when compared with the balls used in the tests with the CrN-coated samples (Fig.  9 b–e). This behavior suggests that, in contact with the untreated alloy, wear occurred predominantly on the disk, as the AISI 52,100 ball exhibits greater mechanical resistance than the Inconel 625 alloy [ 36 ]. In addition, the detection of Ni in the worn region of the ball evidences material transfer from the disk to the counterbody, characterizing adhesive wear associated with the formation of a transfer layer.

Fig. 9 Wear of the tribological pair (ball-on-disk) with elemental mapping showing Ni, Cr, Fe, and O elements: ( a ) UNT, ( b ) PN450, ( c ) PN500, ( d ) CC450, ( e ) CC500, and ( f ) wear profiles of the UNT and CC500 samples

The samples subjected to plasma treatments exhibited narrower wear tracks than the untreated sample (UNT), indicating greater wear resistance of the disk after surface modification. In contrast, the wear scars on the balls corresponding to these samples were larger than those observed with the UNT sample, suggesting greater counterbody wear. This behavior may be attributed to the increased surface hardness of the treated samples, particularly due to the formation of a nitrided layer, which makes the disk surface more resistant and promotes greater material removal from the AISI 52,100 ball during sliding. The elemental mapping of the PN and CC samples indicates a reduction in Ni and Cr signals in the wear-track region, associated with partial removal of the surface layer, and enrichment in Fe and O in the worn regions. The simultaneous presence of Fe and O suggests the formation of an oxidized tribofilm, mainly composed of material transferred from the ball and tribo-oxidative products generated during friction in an oxidizing environment [ 31 ]. This tribofilm may act as an intermediate layer between the contacting surfaces, reducing direct metal-to-metal contact and thereby increasing wear resistance. In the mapping images, the formation of this tribofilm is more evident in samples CC450 and CC500, which may be due to thicker CrN layers and higher surface hardness observed under these conditions. These factors intensify ball wear, promoting greater Fe transfer to the wear track and favoring the formation of a more pronounced tribo-oxidized layer.

The balls used in the tribological contacts with the PN and CC samples exhibited light regions in the worn area, attributed to the accumulation and compaction of oxidized material during sliding. The oxygen enrichment in these regions indicates the formation of an oxidized tribolayer, probably composed mainly of iron oxides derived from the AISI 52,100 ball. The absence of evident Ni and Cr concentrations in the elemental maps suggests that, unlike the UNT sample, material transfer from the disk to the ball was less pronounced, with predominance of counterbody wear and oxidation. In addition, the non-identification of nitrogen in the mapping is due to the technique’s limitations in detecting light elements, particularly the low emission energy of N and the low signal-to-noise ratio in pixel-by-pixel acquisitions [ 37 ]. Thus, the results indicate that contact with the plasma-treated samples favored the formation of an Fe-rich oxidized tribolayer, associated with greater ball wear and higher wear resistance of the modified surfaces.

Figure  9 f compares the cross-sectional profiles of the wear tracks of the UNT and CC500 samples, obtained by roughness/profilometry analysis. The UNT sample exhibited a well-defined wear track, with pronounced depth and a material buildup region at the track edge, likely due to plastic displacement during the test. In contrast, the CC500 sample showed an almost uniform profile, with barely perceptible wear depth compared with the untreated sample, indicating higher wear resistance after the treatment.

The coefficient of friction (CoF) results presented in Fig.  10  indicate that the tribological behavior of the samples is governed by the combination of hardness, roughness, tribofilm formation, and counterbody wear [ 38 ,  39 ]. The UNT sample exhibited the lowest average CoF (0.10 ± 0.02), despite having the lowest surface hardness. This behavior may be associated with its lower roughness and the metallic matrix’s greater ability to accommodate plastic deformation during sliding [ 40 ]. However, this low friction did not result in greater wear resistance, as the wear track on the disk was wider. The plasma-treated samples showed a significant increase in CoF, with average values of 0.60 ± 0.12 for PN450, 0.30 ± 0.11 for PN500, 0.26 ± 0.11 for CC450, and 0.53 ± 0.12 for CC500 (Fig.  10 d). This increase may be attributed to the higher hardness and roughness of the modified surfaces, which intensified the interaction between the asperities of the tribological pair and promoted greater wear of the AISI 52,100 ball.

Fig. 10 Coefficient of friction curves for the ( a ) UNT, ( b ) PN450 and PN500, and ( c ) CC450 and CC500 samples, with smoothed trends. ( d ) Average coefficient of friction values with standard deviation

Fe transfer from the ball and its subsequent oxidation favored the formation of oxidized tribolayers at the interface. In the PN500 and CC450 samples, the lower CoF values for the treated surfaces, particularly 0.26 ± 0.11 for CC450, suggest more stable contact conditions during sliding. This behavior may be associated with the formation of a more continuous tribolayer and a more favorable combination of hardness, roughness, and modified layer thickness. In the case of CC450, although the layer was thick at 6.92 ± 0.99 μm, its roughness was lower than that of CC500, which may have reduced mechanical interlocking between asperities and favored contact stabilization. In contrast, the CC500 sample, despite exhibiting the highest surface hardness and the greatest layer thickness of 7.10 ± 0.54 μm, had a high CoF of 0.53 ± 0.12.

This result indicates that increased hardness and thickness do not necessarily reduce friction, as harder, thicker, and rougher surfaces may promote greater counterbody wear and generate more hard, oxidized debris at the interface [ 40 ]. This debris may act as third-body abrasive particles, increasing the instability of the sliding contact and causing oscillations in the coefficient of friction. Thus, the higher hardness of the treated layers helped reduce disk wear; however, when coupled with higher roughness and the generation of abrasive debris, it also increased the aggressiveness toward the AISI 52,100 ball, directly influencing the evolution and instability of the CoF.

Table  4 ; Fig.  11  present the results of the mass change measured before and after the tribological tests. These data corroborate the SEM/EDS analyses and help explain the mechanisms involved in the formation of tribofilms on the wear tracks. The UNT sample exhibited the highest mass loss on the disk, with a variation of − 4.8 × 10⁻³ g, whereas the corresponding ball showed a much lower mass loss of only − 0.1 × 10⁻³ g. This behavior indicates that, upon contact with the untreated sample, wear occurred predominantly on the Inconel 625 disk, consistent with the greater wear-track width observed by SEM and the lower surface hardness of the metallic matrix. Thus, although the UNT sample exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction, this result was not associated with higher wear resistance, since significant material removal occurred from the disk.

On the other hand, the plasma-treated samples showed much smaller mass variations in the disk. For the PN450, PN500, and CC450 samples, a slight apparent mass gain of approximately + 0.2 × 10⁻³ g was even observed. This gain should not be interpreted as the absence of wear, but rather as evidence of material retention and compaction on the wear track after the test. This behavior is associated with the formation of tribofilms composed primarily of material transferred from the AISI 52,100 ball (mainly Fe) and tribo-oxidative products generated during sliding. This interpretation is consistent with the EDS results, which indicated enrichment of Fe and O in the worn regions of the treated samples. Therefore, the slight mass increase observed in the treated disks suggests that the mass incorporated into the surface through material transfer and oxidation may have compensated for, or even slightly exceeded, the mass removed during wear.

For the balls, the mass variations were very small, ranging from 0.0 to − 0.1 × 10⁻³ g for the treated samples. This indicates that material loss from the counterbody was low in absolute terms or was partially compensated by the adhesion of debris and oxidized products to the wear scar. However, the SEM images showed larger wear scars on the balls used against the PN and CC samples, indicating significant surface modification of the counterbody, despite the measured mass variation being small.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The application of conventional plasma nitriding (PN) and cathodic cage plasma nitriding (CCPN) techniques to Inconel 625 promoted the formation of CrN-rich surface layers, owing to chromium’s greater chemical affinity for nitrogen than nickel. The CCPN method demonstrated greater efficiency in producing thick (~ 7 μm) and homogeneous layers, since the shielding effect of the cage minimizes direct ion bombardment and the surface sputtering effect that limits layer growth in the PN process. This microstructural modification induced lattice contraction of the NiCr matrix and crystallite refinement, both of which directly contributed to the increase in surface hardness.

The mechanical and tribological tests confirmed the effectiveness of the treatments, particularly in the CC500 condition, which showed a 383.7% increase in hardness relative to the untreated material. Although all conditions showed good adhesion, the layers produced at 450 °C, particularly CC450, demonstrated greater structural integrity (HF1), whereas those produced at 500 °C exhibited greater brittleness and a higher susceptibility to cracking under load. In terms of wear behavior, the formation of Fe- and O-rich protective tribofilms, originating from material transferred from the AISI 52,100 counterbody, resulted in a drastic reduction in mass loss of the nitrided components.

In terms of chemical stability, nitriding rendered the Inconel 625 surface electrochemically more noble in a saline medium. The conventional technique (PN450) exhibited the best corrosion resistance due to its lower surface roughness, which hinders the initiation of localized corrosion processes caused by the retention of aggressive species. Based on these results, the plasma surface modification method shows high potential for application in naval components, consolidating itself as an economical, sustainable, and efficient alternative to electrolytic chromium and HVOF for increasing the durability and reliability of structures subjected to harsh marine environments.
